title: Process States: Running, Ready, Blocked
topic: Process states — a process is always in one of three states: RUNNING on the CPU, READY waiting for the CPU, or BLOCKED waiting on an I/O completion; the scheduler and I/O events drive every transition

beats.narration: Where is your program right this second — on the CPU, waiting in line, or stuck on a disk read?

elements.content: Every process lives in one of three states.

beats.narration: RUNNING — currently on the CPU. READY — eligible to run, but the CPU is busy. BLOCKED — waiting on something else, like a disk to finish.

elements.content: Three rectangular state boxes: RUNNING (amber), READY (chalk), BLOCKED (rose)
Single thread token sits in RUNNING
the OS bookkeeps every process by this label

beats.narration: When the scheduler's time slice expires, the running process is descheduled to ready, and a ready process is scheduled to running.

elements.content: Arrows between RUNNING and READY labelled 'descheduled' / 'scheduled'
Token P1 leaves RUNNING and slides to READY
Token P2 (already in READY) slides up to RUNNING
the scheduler picks who runs next

beats.narration: If the running process asks for I/O, it leaves the CPU and enters the blocked state. When the disk finishes, the process moves back to ready, eligible to run again.

elements.content: Token P2 makes an I/O request — slides from RUNNING to BLOCKED
After disk completes, token slides from BLOCKED to READY (not RUNNING)
I/O completion sends you back to the ready queue, not straight to the CPU

beats.narration: Three states — running, ready, blocked. Two drivers of motion — the scheduler and the I/O subsystem. That's how every process moves through the OS.
